tokens.v: An open-ended planning training session: a sales order becomes demand, MRP turns demand into planned orders, planned orders transfer into real purchase and production orders, and those get received through to put-away. Two extra wrinkles got explored along the way — a contract-based order type that behaves differently from a sales order, and a live puzzle about why a safety-stock top-up seemed to split into three orders instead of one.

topics.title: Demand shows up before you plan for it

tokens.v: The moment a sales order line is saved, it's visible as demand — no planning run needed to see it. You do still need to run MRP ("Generate Orders") to turn that demand into an actual planned production or purchase order.

blocks.text: The moment a sales order line is saved, it's visible as demand — no planning run needed to see it. You do still need to run MRP ("Generate Orders") to turn that demand into an actual planned production or purchase order.

tokens.v: Receiving happens in stages: receive → confirm → (if the warehouse uses locations) advise a location → put away. Confirming isn't the same as putting away.

topics.title: A second kind of demand: contract deliverables

tokens.v: Sales orders aren't the only thing that can drive planning. A "contract deliverable" can too — but it behaves differently.

blocks.text: Sales orders aren't the only thing that can drive planning. A "contract deliverable" can too — but it behaves differently.

tokens.v: What was shown:

Unlike a sales order (recognized by planning the instant it's created), a contract deliverable sits inactive until someone deliberately activates it. Left inactive, MRP ignores it completely, with no warning.

items.text: Unlike a sales order (recognized by planning the instant it's created), a contract deliverable sits inactive until someone deliberately activates it. Left inactive, MRP ignores it completely, with no warning.

tokens.v: Once activated, it plans and ships the same way a sales order would, but it's tagged to a specific project the whole way through — the production order made for it is "pegged" to that one contract.

items.text: Once activated, it plans and ships the same way a sales order would, but it's tagged to a specific project the whole way through — the production order made for it is "pegged" to that one contract.

topics.title: The safety-stock puzzle (see the dedicated write-up)

tokens.v: A safety-stock question from this same session — why setting safety stock to 50 for a test item seemed to generate three separate orders instead of one — is written up separately, since it got fully resolved afterward in a chat thread. Short version: it wasn't really a safety-stock problem at all. Only one of the three orders was actually tied to safety stock; the other two were ordinary orders for two unrelated sales orders that just happened to be sitting in the same list.
